I moved from Milan to a town of four thousand people, and the first thing I noticed was that nobody here is anonymous. At seven in the morning the square is already full. The stallholders arrive before six, and by seven there is a gruff old man with a weathered face selling tomatoes, and a chatty woman selling flowers who knows everything about everybody. I thought I would keep to myself. That lasted two weeks. Somebody knocked on my door with a plate of food, and after that I was a regular in three different shops. Is it tiring? Sometimes. Word gets around here in a single morning. But when my mother was ill, four people I barely knew came to the house. In Milan I lived eleven years in the same building and I never learned one single name.

People ask me whether I miss the small town I grew up in, and the honest answer is that I miss the people and not the town. Two thousand four hundred people, one traffic light, and a diner where the same six men have had breakfast at the same table since before I was born. When I was seventeen I found the whole thing exhausting. Everybody knew what I did on Friday before I got home on Saturday. Then I moved to a city of three million, and for two years nobody said my name in the street. Now I go back twice a year, and the same waitress still calls me by my father's name. It is not the buildings I go back for. It is that somebody notices when you are not there.
